Hi [~accountid:61b9ad772960d2006976792c] 

Sharing you the overviewed agreement: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jA4J5aSogJfKZgLckyf9hVLi8-Y2pRie/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jA4J5aSogJfKZgLckyf9hVLi8-Y2pRie/edit|smart-link] 

 After discussing also with my colleagues *we strongly recommend to not use automatic renewal they have proposed*. +*Instead*+ *we can use reversed type of renewal which basically means that if we notify them 30 days prior to the end of the Subscription Term that we want to extend the subscription then it is doable.* +Especially since they didn´t agree with the termination right we proposed, which means that we basically don´t have any safeguards for ourselves in a case if we are not happy with their service or purely just don´t need it,+ at the same time they do have every security that service is bought in buy us nevertheless the circumstances. 

Under my proposed renewal clause their business model is secured (so plus for them) and our risks are also secured (e.g if we see that we want the change the service provider or just don´t need the info anymore, etc), so win-win for both parties. 

*Why we recommend not to have automatic renewal in the way they proposed?*

i. since they are new partner then they haven´t proven their reliability (quality) yet,

ii. with these type of automatic renewals it may happen that the person who was responsible for buying that type of service in and renewing the need for it  is on the vacation, doesn't´t work in the team anymore or just forgets to send the prior notice to not renew the subscription. This results us to be tied with the service provider and obliged to pay money for them for a whole year in a case where we don´t want or need their service anymore.  That is why, we recommend to have rather this reversed renewal process that  I explained above and also added into the contract.

iii. Since they are the service providers then they should be interested to get a new and big client who may potentially buy in more service from them. Hence, it is logical for them to make a compromise from which both parties win. 

Liisa

Hey [~accountid:5d50390ec6b9320d9ea58352] 

So first of all we have 2 different definitions of debt. More details can be found here [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/4701619012/Debt+Analytics+in+Billing+101#Overview|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/4701619012/Debt+Analytics+in+Billing+101#Overview|smart-link] but on a high level:

# Billing definition → debt is generated only after the invoice issued has gone overdue (e.g. for drivers it’s usually 7th for the previous month)
# Finance definition → debt is generated after 1 day (e.g. driver takes cash ride today & debt is generated tomorrow for this order) 

Let me know against which definition do you mean to monitor here? 

My proposal here’s to use the 2. Finance definition as we’re talking about AB testing where the experiments most probably will not last several months. 

Also we unfortunately don’t have historical debt amounts available & everything we see is debt today → is this a blocker? Could you please let me know which fields the Experimentation platform needs to add this metric to the scorecard? As a first version maybe we can use something like this:

{noformat}select 
etl.entity_type as type,
etl.entity_id as driver_id,
etl.currency as currency,
sum(etl.amount_due/cer.rate - etl.amount_paid/cer.rate) as current_debt_eur,
sum(etl.amount_due - etl.amount_paid) as current_debt_loc,
max(etl.created_date) as last_activity
from ng_public.etl_billing_debt_driver_v2 etl
left join ng_public.currency_exchange_rates cer on cer.currency = etl.currency and cer.valid_on = etl.created_date 
where etl.entity_type = 'driver' -- 'driver_fleet' for fleets
and etl.currency = 'ghs'
group by 1,2,3
limit 100{noformat}

Hi [~accountid:60bd1bad00bdd900683be69c] and [~accountid:5bdbfc9b359ddf204e8c7e02] 

Just had a meeting with [~accountid:5d4283c94125b20c3159c0dc] where he explained the background of your inquiry and explained your plans. As I explained to Daniel then, +alcohol icon itself can be removed separately from the warning text, if necessary, BUT the warning text near the alcoholic beverage+ (so that it could be seen easily when specific alcoholic product is displayed) +must maintain+ due to legal requirements (based on the table). Thereat, warning text exact context may vary a bit country by country (as seen from the [table|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1gI-GsiCkIqV9vvyEPbRk0BhRXXfCSa8HqmTkPdRi5Lc/edit#gid=1218586163]), but generally is quite similar and usually varied by the age numbers and by the fact that in some countries text is prescribed exactly in the law (e.g. in Estonia) and in others exact format is left more free and only content requirements are foreseen (e.g. Latvia). 

We also discussed with Daniel whether it would help us out if we would tell some/all merchants to add these warning texts by themselves, but as I explained to Daniel, then even if we put contractually all responsibility to merchants it may not save us from liability or some requirements. Hence, we came to a conclusion that it is probably easier to add this warning text by ourselves not keep our fingers crossed that merchants always add this text exactly where needed. 

I also understood that for [~accountid:5bdbfc9b359ddf204e8c7e02]  it wasn´t maybe very clear whether these requirements apply also to our platform. +General answer would be that yes, we are liable or there is very high risk of us being liable (depending on the market).+ Although it isn´t always explicitly stated in the law that platform is liable, then it can be derived from different legal requirements, case law and also from new developments in legislation which put more and more responsibility to platforms. Based on aforementioned and also the fact that the sale of alcoholic products is very regulated area, then the risk for not displaying warning texts clearly and easily near the product itself carries a very high risk for us being non-compliant. 

The decision is of course made by you and if you want to discuss this topic more thoroughly, then please let me know 🙏 We can also include respective GFT members for specific markets, but getting answer from them takes probably some time due to their workloads. 

Liisa

Hello, I will be closing this ticket, please take up the conversation in a dedicated food analytics channel/service desk if anything is still needed from that side 🙏

Here is some information on how card data is ingested and used in our platform. I hoped it will be described by relevant Commerce team in order to avoid me missing details how data flows, but here it is as I know (this is not detailed information): 

* User adds payment instrument in the application by entering card details into relevant form
* Application posts this data to dedicated service platform - [pci.bolt.eu|http://pci.bolt.eu] - where
** card details are forwarded to card tokenisation service Processout, we receive token that is stored in our platform and this can be used for card transactions without card details by our payment processing system
** card PAN is masked (some digits replaced with “*” according to requirements of the PCI DSS standard) and sent to our backend database along with token received in previous step
** our databases store only masked data along with card expiration date and owners name as entered in the form
* Under full PCI DSS compliance scope is all parts of system where full card data is exposed
** Applications with card detail entry form
** [pci.bolt.eu|http://pci.bolt.eu] environment
* If we want to change anything in the system by exposing full card details anywhere else in the system, or add persons having access, or add buildings where people having access to this data work or where the data itself is processed-stored, will fall automatically under the scope of PCI compliance requirements
* PCI DSS compliance means continuous monitoring of changes and testing of systems and preparing 6 months for yearly audit along with validating that processes established for security and compliance, are working, including:
** complying with physical requirements in case card data is exposed in physical premises, we have minimised the scope for Bolt so that this does not apply to us right now
** doing background checks of all people involved in data processing (including engineers who manage, operate or design the system)
** making sure all relevant employees pass PCI scope relevant training
** making sure devices used by people in scope for work comply with requirements
** and many many things more, as new version of the PCI standard influences org chart, roles, segregation of duties, risk management and whatnotelse topics.

So - when I say that there is theoretical possibility to extract full data then I was not kidding - in order to start extracting data we would need to expand our PCI scope significantly with ridiculous increase in expense to make sure the data is secured according to requirements of the standard. 

We have chosen to minimise the PCI scope and keep in our databases only the data that is absolutely minimal to do business (process payments) and we mask sensitive data in order to keep both PCI DSS and GDPR gods happy and contribute to the profitability of Bolt.

Hey [~accountid:63b29b637cde7bff9d796748] unfortunately we don’t have an easy way to put everything onto 1 report but let me go through how I imagine the process would work for you.

Let’s say you want to fetch this data for couriers in Tartu, Estonia for Dec 2023 right.



First of all I’d run this report [https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/looks/26182?toggle=fil,pik|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/looks/26182?toggle=fil,pik] & filter:
{{Created Date is before absolute 2023/12/01}} → this gives us the courier current balance as of 30th Nov 2023 (you can also check the field Last Update which shows the timestamp of the last balance entry included to the report) 
These values will be your {{Opening Balance}} numbers

Then I’d run this report [https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/looks/26181?toggle=fil&qid=epjzYfSlUqPT8sEEUyNB2A|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/looks/26181?toggle=fil&qid=epjzYfSlUqPT8sEEUyNB2A] & filter:
{{Created Local Date is in the last 1 complete months}} → this gives us the numbers on bag deposits for Tartu in Dec 2023 (you can check the Month field which shows you the month this data is for). You can also query longer timeframe here if needed, the report is pivoted over month

Finally I’d go back to this report [https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/looks/26182?toggle=fil,pik&qid=fzqqIWpdHbSM9ysh5Jt7v7|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/looks/26182?toggle=fil,pik&qid=fzqqIWpdHbSM9ysh5Jt7v7] but this time filter:
{{Created Date is before absolute 2024/01/01}} → this gives us the courier current balance as of 31st Dec 2023 (check the Last Update field again to validate your filtering is correct)
These values will be your {{Closing Balance}} numbers

This:

* adds dependency within API clients (not sure how bad it is),
* adds necessity to use {{t*}} types within component test.



I see two possible outcomes:

* when generating {{gen/componentTest}} just replace {{@server-api-async}} imports with the ones from {{@server-component-test}}?
* or probably better — copy type definitions completely to be located within single file (so no imports from other files except for njsc ones).

+*Summary of the advice provided by Burness Paull on Bolt withholding payment from Drivers where there is suspected fraud*+

* There is no UK legislation that specifically permits or prohibits  the withholding of payments where fraud has occurred in a business to business context. 
* In order to provide protection against fraud contractually Bolt needs to specifically address this in the driver General terms and conditions  and also consider the implications  of the _Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977_ (“UCTA”).

+*Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (“UCTA”)*+

* Self-employed independent contractors have some protection against unfair contract terms in business-to-business contracts under the UCTA. 
* UCTA regulates the exclusion and restriction of liability for breach of express and implied contractual obligations and allows for arguments that certain clauses in a contract may be considered unfair or unreasonable and as a result could be unenforceable.
* UCTA also contains anti-evasion provisions designed to catch clauses that may not expressly limit liability but achieve a similar effect, including excusing a party from non-performance of its own standard terms. A clause that excuses a party from performing its own standard written terms (e.g., payment) must be reasonable to be enforceable (Section 3 (2) (b), UCTA).
* The following sets out some clauses to consider in the drafting of the Driver General terms and conditions.



*Set off clause* 

# A set off clause should ideally be included in the Driver General terms and conditions so that Bolt have a contractual right to set off any liability (present or future/contingent, liquidated or unliquidated and whether or not the liability arose under the contract) and therefore retain funds held by Bolt on behalf of a driver in the event that a fraud is discovered.
# The drafting and application of the clause would need to be considered carefully to ensure it passed the UCTA reasonableness test. A number of other considerations would also need to be taken into account such as the specific circumstances and timing of triggering the set off.

*Interest clause*

# There is no contractual entitlement currently for drivers to receive interest on late payments in the Driver General terms and conditions.

*Therefore, if Bolt do decide to withhold payments and there is a determination later that there was no fraud or that the withholding of payment was unreasonable, drivers may seek to rely on the* *_Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998_* *on the unpaid sums under which they could be entitled to 8% above the Bank of England base rate plus an administration fee.*

+*Penalties*+

# The general rule is that if a clause is a penalty, it will not be enforced beyond the actual loss of the innocent party.  A clause may be penal if it imposes a detriment on the contract-breaker that is out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in enforcing the primary obligation.
# The rule against penalties will apply to a clause that disentitles the party in breach from receiving a sum which would otherwise be due to him. 
# Bolt should consider the likelihood of the sums being withheld from the drivers being more than the loss suffered by Bolt due to fraud, as the drivers may benefit from the rule that penalty clauses are not enforceable.

+*Damages*+ 

# Should payments due to the drivers be withheld, there is a risk that drivers may take civil action against Bolt to recover lost revenue. Therefore, it is important that Bolt have a quick and thorough investigation process in place to ensure that any sums that are legitimately due to drivers after the investigation can be repaid promptly.
# Although it is unlikely that a driver would sue for loss if they have committed fraud, Bolt should also consider the potential reputational damage if the public becomes aware that Bolt are withholding payments to drivers.

+*EMPLOYMENT LAW / RECLASSIFICATION CONSIDERATONS*+

# If there was to be a reclassification of drivers (either as a result of litigation or a decision made by Bolt) to worker (or employee) status, then whether deductions from their pay are permitted would need to be considered through the lens of the unlawful deduction from wages regime set out in the Employment Rights Act 1996. This legislation provides that it is unlawful for an employer to make a deduction from a worker’s wages unless (i) the deduction is required or authorised by statute or a provision in the worker’s contract; or (ii) the worker has given their prior written consent to the deduction. 

The current version of the ‘General Terms: Drivers’ section 7 says that:

“Not complying with the Acceptable Use Policy is a serious breach of these Terms and will entitle Bolt UK to take any of the following actions (with or without notice, subject always to section 9); […] withholding or permanently denying any payments payable to you as a result of prohibited behaviour that does not comply with the Fraud Policy. In these circumstances, your right to appeal such a decision is set out in the Fraud Policy”  

If drivers were to bring claims of unlawful deductions from wages, the Tribunal would consider the terms of the contract in place and (assuming the Tribunal were content to accept the wording at section 5.3 formed part of their contract as a worker or employee) then making a deduction from pay when a driver is found to have committed fraud could be said to have been ‘required or authorised… by a provision in the worker’s contract’. Difficulties may arise, however, if the driver disputes that they have committed fraud. In this scenario, whether the deduction is lawful or not will depend on the robustness of the company’s checks and investigations into the allegations of fraud as the company would need to be able to demonstrate that the event justifying the deduction has, as a matter of fact, occurred. It will therefore be advisable to ensure such allegations are thoroughly investigated before a deduction is made from drivers’ remuneration.  

The financial exposure of an unlawful deduction claim is somewhat quantifiable as it generally amounts to the sum that has been ‘unlawfully deducted’. Technically, a Tribunal can also award a sum that it considers appropriate to compensate any financial loss sustained by the individual, but any such loss must be attributable to the deduction and is therefore limited to things like bank charges, or interest if the deduction caused the worker’s bank account to be overdrawn, etc. There is otherwise no additional remedy available in such claims unless the individual was to raise another type of claim such as discrimination.

+*SUMMARY*+

* There is no current UK legislation that we are aware of that specifically permits or prohibits the withholding of payments held on behalf of drivers where fraud is suspected or discovered.
* However, due to the potential application of UCTA to Bolt’s contracts with Drivers, where they are independent contractors, there is no definitive way to ensure contractually that Bolt may permanently retain payments they hold for drivers in the event that fraud is suspected or discovered.
* Specific contractual protections are potentially available and should be included but all will need to be drafted carefully against UCTA.
* From an employment law perspective, if drivers are reclassified as workers or employees (either through litigation or as a result of Bolt choosing this relationship going forward), deductions as a result of fraud could be challenged by way of a claim for unlawful deduction from wages in the Employment Tribunal. Given the current terms in place, Bolt would have a stateable defence to such claims in the Tribunal, but the success of the defence would be hinged on there being sufficient evidence of fraud.

+*Advice to the business*+ 

* To mitigate against any potential civil claims that may be brought by Drivers who want to recover loss revenue it is imperative that Bolt have a quick and thorough fraud process in place to investigate any fraudulent activity. As previously advised, we suggest keeping a record (retaining documents and evidence) when there is a suspected fraud, having this information on file will assist Bolt defend if a claim is made.
* Although it is unlikely that a driver would sue for loss if they have committed fraud, Bolt should also consider the potential reputational damage if the public becomes aware that Bolt are withholding payments to drivers.

+*Suggestions by Burness Paull*+

* Burness Paull has recommended that the Driver terms and conditions are reviewed considering the contractual protections available, any drafting would need to be considered against UCTA.
* In the event Bolt decides to voluntarily reclassify drivers as workers or employees, Burness Paull can assist with the drafting of specific wording in those new contracts to ensure any deduction for fraud is, on the face of it, permitted under the contract.

Here is how finding the corresponding payment works:

*ArnFilter*:

{noformat}arn_payment: 
  ethoca_alert ea
  => payment_notification pn (pn.arn = ea.arn)
      => payment_payment_row ppr (ppr.id = pn.payment_row_id)
        => ppr.payment_id 

Execution time:
1. look for row with given ARN (0 or 1) in arn_payment
2. Use payment ID if found{noformat}

*MerchantDescriptorFilter*:

{noformat}merchant_descriptor_payment:
  ethoca_alert ea
  => payment_request_log prl (ea.card_bin + ea.soft_descriptor)
      => payment_row ppr (ppr.id = prl.payment_row_id)
          => payment p (p.id = ppr.payment_id)

Execution time:
1. look for all rows with given card_bin + merchant_descriptor in merchant_descriptor_payment
2. For each row:
      match converted currency amount, time, card_last4.
3. Use payment ID if 1 match, otherwise return []{noformat}

*AmountFilter:*

{noformat}1. Load all payments by user
   based on card_bin, last4, time window
2. For each user payment: match currency and amount
3. If 1 match: use payment ID, otherwise return []{noformat}

*ConvertedAmountFilter:*

{noformat}1. Use user payment data from AmountFilter
2. For each user payment: convert currency, then match amount
3. If 1 match: use payment ID, otherwise return []{noformat}

*CardAliasFilter:*

{noformat}1. Use user payment data from AmountFilter
2. Are all the payments from 1 card alias? If yes, use all of them{noformat}

HI

This is the result of the dynamic commission, the calculation of monthly commission does this way that  we are taking less commission from the driver because we are subtracting from the total Fee (App orders) - all bonuses/compensations/ride discounts

To calculate ride discounts ( need to export all orders for the same period and calculated the difference between the client payed and the ride price)

This is due to a new invoicing system we gradually started to in Spain 01-05-23 called Dynamic Commission. Drivers' or Fleets' bonuses are now aggregated in their commission and the final sum is displayed only as one row: commission row. For example;

Commission: 100€, Bonuses 25€, Booking Fee 15€, Refunds 10€

Driver will only see a single row in their commission invoice in the amount of 50€ (100-25-15-10).

So, technically [actual commission - bounses/compensations - rider discounts - booking fees = commission on the invoice]

the report show the gross commission (the report shows the commission before all these discounts). on the invoice, the amount is all other things deducted from it (since commission netting is active). So actual commission invoice will never match with report.

Basically:

Commission invoice - the final sum of commission that  shows for the monthly period, how much commission we took from the driver in the end (after refunds, some of their bonuses/compensation, and rider discounts have been deducte- so this is Driver’s expenses this done to decrease Driver’s commission in the end.

But report and app expenses, shows gross amount that that driver owes to us before we deduct refunds/bonuses/compensations/ ride discounts. 

More info about dynamic commission [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/3663265890].

In this case commission (687.6 eur) - Campaign compensation (694.3 eur) = -6.7

[~accountid:607a94cf115da6006f750793] this happens in this case, it is not really bug, by design it is done this wayWhen you upload/clone bulk group you can calculate costs and *it will apply* when you *create* the bulk group.But if you already *create* the bulk group with empty costs and then press calculate costs it will only display in UI calculated costs, but it will not be saved because the bulk group *has been already created.*So if you want to apply the costs, calculate the costs before creating the bulk group, otherwise it will be only *informative* information.There is 2 ways we can solve this
A) We will disable the cost calculation for the created bulk groups to avoid confusion
B) We can try to apply/override the costs for the bulk groups if it is in *created state* too, it will require backend/UI changes

Sent out response to police.

We won’t support multi-worker setup (at least in the scope of builder migration to Kubernetes epic). Multi-worker configuration is tightly coupled with in-memory worker state, which results in different issues when running multiple workers or/and doing worker state changes (e.g. stopping one worker). 

Multi-worker setup also creates problems related to the traffic distribution between worker instances. We need to make changes to the service discovery to omit forwarding traffic to stopped workers or we need to completely uncouple worker state with builder API, which might be time consuming and introduce additional risks.

We will continue migration to Kubernetes with our initial plan - carefully test all cases on prelive and afterwards migrate live.

Hello [~accountid:712020:0b672045-ccee-47bd-a209-1bec8346b45c], 

payout = total earnings - commission

commission invoice = commission

total earnings = total revenue - all expenses + all additional incomes

In rides report, it shows only earnings from the orders, while we should also consider the fee we deducted, campaigns that drivers enrolled and other expenses/incomes.

For example, if one driver made 100 rides in one month, each ride is worth 1 EUR, and he enrolled one campaign that gives him 100 EUR when he finishes 100 rides, the commission rate is 20%, each ride we charge 1% fee, and all rides are paid by card:

Total earnings = 100 * 1 - 100 * 1% - 100 * 20% + 100 = 179 EUR

Total revenue(aka rides report) = 100 * 1 = 100 EUR

commission = 100 * 20% = 20 EUR

payout = 179 - 20 = 159 EUR

Hope this helps you understand better on the difference between payout and commission.

In some cases we generate the invoices as “hidden” invoices - they do exist in the system with the subtype “statement” and they are hidden (they are not sent to the riders, they cannot be downloaded from the Rider App and they cannot be downloaded from the Admin Panel either).

First case - the “Send invoice info for cash payment method” option is unchecked on the company’s profile. In this case the invoices are hidden for payment methods where the rider pays directly to the driver on the spot after the ride (cash or card terminal).

Second case - the issuer and the recipient are the same. It’s not legal to issue an invoice to oneself so in case the driver's registry code and the rider’s registry code are identical, the invoice will be hidden.

Looks like we have a race condition in our cancel+notification(authorisation) logic, here’s the flow:

# [notfication] successful authorisation notification request start
# [cancel] request start
# === race condition start
# [cancel] taking data from db, payment is pending authorisation
# [notification] handle the notification, update payment to authorised state
# [cancel] based on old data we only update stateGoal to {{reversed}} [here|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/30eb408d875cb8c8aa8c2d90b5edfa1c9cb2c0e5/src/platform/payment/payment_core/main/service/router/cancel.ts#L194]
# === race condition end
# [notification] OK response
# [cancel] OK response
# after that nothing happens. Normally we would start the “reverseLater” cancel process during notification handling, but since here it happened before the stateGoal was changed, so nothing happens



Options to fix:

# In cancel, check that payment has not changed state. If it did - throw {{OPTIMISTIC_CONCURRENCY_ERROR}} and wait for caller to retry
# In cancel, [before making a decision|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/30eb408d875cb8c8aa8c2d90b5edfa1c9cb2c0e5/src/platform/payment/payment_core/main/service/router/cancel.ts#L172] start a transaction, to make sure that data will no be changed before we set new stateGoal

After an investigation it looks like the timeouts did come from down stream when Google or Internal Provider had some hiccups. For the volume of request that the routing provider serve, this level of timeouts is peanuts(<0.1%) but for the getAccurateEtas endpoint it can be a big value considering the low volume of calls.

The strange thing that I didn’t understand is why only getAccurateEtas endpoint is affected while getEtas is not or much less(both call the same endpoint from geo-routing). If I think more about it, getEtas is configured to timeout after 2 seconds when is just calling drivingDistanceMatrix endpoint while getAccurateEtas is configured to timeout after 2 seconds calling dDM and model-invoker. So the most obvious conclusion is that the extra processing of the server(that can be measured with the event loop lag) takes some share of time and it excede the SLA of 2 seconds.

The obvious solution for this is to increase the configured timeout from 2 sec to 2.5 sec to give more headroom for the processing that is taking place on the server.

{noformat}WITH partner_data AS (
SELECT
driver_id,
partner_id,
first_finished_order AS partner_activation_datetime
FROM ng_public.etl_partner_data
WHERE driver_id IS NOT NULL AND partner_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1,2,3),

lead_data AS (
SELECT
fdrl.created AS lead_created_date,
fdrl.id AS lead_id,
fdrl.driver_id, 
fdrl.is_duplicate AS lead_is_duplicate,
admin_city.name AS city, -- registration city
admin_country.name AS country, -- registration country
max(e2.created) AS step_2_created
FROM
ng_public.fleet_driver_registration_log fdrl
LEFT JOIN ng_public.fleet_driver_registration_event e2 ON e2.driver_registration_log_id=fdrl.id AND e2.step='step_2' AND e2.created >= fdrl.created
LEFT JOIN ng_public.admin_system_city admin_city ON admin_city.id = fdrl.city_id
LEFT JOIN ng_public.admin_system_country admin_country ON admin_city.country_code  = admin_country.code
WHERE fdrl.created_date >= date('2023-05-01')
GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5,6),


combined AS (
SELECT
lead_data.*,
partner_data.driver_id,
partner_data.partner_id,
partner_data.partner_activation_datetime,
MIN(lead_created_date) OVER (PARTITION BY partner_id) AS earliest_lead_created_date
FROM lead_data
LEFT JOIN partner_data ON partner_data.driver_id = lead_data.driver_id
),


combined_2 AS (
SELECT
combined.*,
date_diff('day',date(earliest_lead_created_date), date(partner_activation_datetime)) AS lead_to_activation_days
FROM combined)



SELECT
date(lead_created_date) AS date,
combined_2.country,
combined_2.city,
count(DISTINCT lead_id) AS signups,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step_2_created IS NOT NULL THEN lead_id END) AS step_2,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date AND lead_to_activation_days <= 14 THEN partner_id END) AS activations_14d,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date AND lead_to_activation_days <= 21 THEN partner_id END) AS activations_21d,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date AND lead_to_activation_days <= 30 THEN partner_id END) AS activations_30d,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date THEN partner_id END) AS activations
FROM combined_2
WHERE combined_2.city IN ('Lisbon')
GROUP BY 1,2,3
order by 1{noformat}

Hi [~accountid:712020:341b8095-1e4f-44ea-ad93-e6b03a07da4c] , please find my answers to your questions below:

* *1 & 2*:

||*Scenario*||*Advise*||
|*_Existing_* *employees &* {color:#ff991f}*private*{color} *devices*|We should avoid relying on consent. In such cases, the best alternate legal basis would be our “*legitimate interests*” (on the basis that we are protecting our confidential and proprietary information).|
|*_Former_* *employees &* {color:#ff991f}*private*{color} *devices*|We should rely on *consent* in the first instance. In such cases, we should use the consent form drafted. If a device is not in our possession, we should request the device to be sent back to our offices and then continue to rely on *consent* in the first instance. 
If a former employee refuses to provide consent to access their device (physically/remotely/virtually), we can potentially justify accessing the device based on our *legitimate interests*.|
|*_Existing_* *and* *_Former_* *employees &* {color:#4c9aff}*work*{color} *devices*|We don’t require consent to access a work device and shouldn’t ask for it from a current employee. Former employees could grant consent, but it wouldn’t be necessary. In both cases, we would rely on Bolt’s *legitimate interests* to access work devices in our possession.|

* *3*: there is no specific legal requirement around how we would store the device. I mentioned this as an alternative ‘last resort' where an employee has not provided us with their consent to access their device and has not requested the device back. In this case, we would want to archive it securely so that no one else can access the employee’s data on their device, and our data is also secured. However, my recommendation before this would be for us to then get permission to wipe the device as opposed to accessing it and browsing through it.

Can you let me know what has been agreed about accessing the device (with permission) versus wiping it entirely (with permission) — what does/will the policy say? In my view, wiping the device entirely without actually browsing its contents will always be a safer and ‘privacy-preserving’ method to securing our copied data.

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *17/12/2023.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

*Your rights*

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. To answer to both of your questions:

* _You mentioned that Central Operations, Product and Supplier management teams in HQ, and Team Leads should all be working with this data — please explain why anyone other than the employee’s manager should have access to that specific employee’s performance data?_
** Agree - in general only the manager should see the *person level* access. Central teams are interested in *country level* statistics usually to build and develop processes and features (for example automated flows for accepting drivers or task management tooling in Beehive). The only time where we’d need individual level access is to dive deeper into market performance. We do performance tracking on a global level to identify outlier markets and help them improve and in this case it would be helpful to see if the poor performance of a market is caused by some outlier specialists within the team. If this is a concern from Privacy side though then we can rely on the team lead to give us insights into the market's high or poor performance. 
* _please share current regulation of employee duties in employment contract/job description in connection with this request?_
** I’m not aware of any regulation. Do you mean some local laws or EU regulation or what?
* _Are there any KPIs set for specific tasks already? If yes what are they, where and how they are communicated to the employees and how they will change with implementation of this project_
** Tracking the performance is mainly expected to cover the work that outsourced providers do. We still have some in-house teams doing the work though so that’s why I wanted to double check with you. We will eventually be in a place where these tasks will not be done by in-house teams (hopefully by EOY). When it comes to outsourcing providers it’s easier: performance management is already or would be added to the contract/T&C of the provider. That’s where Supplier management team comes into play. Since they manage the providers as suppliers and manage their performance, they would need the access on an individual level to hold the providers accountable.
** I am working out the KPIs but on an individual level they will most probably be:
*** Accuracy of work. Measured either in Error rate or First Time Right. This basically means if the agents filled in the information/processed the document correctly the first time. 
*** Speed/volume of tasks. Measured in X% of tasks completed within Y timeframe.
** There would be a certain threshold/target we apply for the KPIs. If the provider or the individual don’t meet the target for a certain period, we would hold the agents accountable and have the outsourced provider work on fixing the issue or replacing the agents. In-house teams would manage the decision making on their employees on their own but central teams can make recommendations on how to improve their processes in general.

Second case - the issuer and the recipient are the same. It’s not legal to issue an invoice to oneself so in case the driver's registry code and the rider’s registry code are identical, the invoice will be hidden.

To continue the topic of Credible intervals:

[Github for Step 1 and Step 2|https://github.com/bolteu/data-analytics/blob/master/marketing/adhocs/%5BMarTech-5774%5D_comparing_ci.ipynb]

*Step 1: Reproduce CausalPy solutions* 
Made sure that with a regular PyMC API I am able to reproduce not only the predictions and daily credible intervals, but also the cumulative intervals.
Reproducing the code might sound trivial, but here I did not copy the code, but wrote my own and compared to CausalPy to understand in which places we’re thinking differently
In the files below most important plot is one where PyMC sampling cumulative and CausalPy are the same. (picture shows example of [Madrid experiment|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/4518313985/2023-06+Madrid+iOS+multiple+channels+Budget+Increase])

!CausalPy and PyMC Sampling Cumulative are same.png|width=710,height=511!



[^Check Conf Intervals - mu.zip]



*Step 2: Decide how to calculate uncertainty*

CausalPy uses mu to create credible intervals.

However, 

* mu seems to resemble more what in frequentist setup would be confidence intervals, while y_hat would be the prediction intervals.
In other words, mu seems to only encompass the uncertainty of what could be our general prediction line. y_hat, on the other hand, also takes to account the uncertainty related to the error that the model made (sigma). That’s why posteriors of mu have less variance than those of y_hat.
* Additionally, mu grows linearly as you consider more days (given priors are the same) (most probably due to its deterministic nature). And we do not expect it to be so. As we have shown [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH-5814]{color:#ff5630}, {color}variance should grow with some pace resembling sqrt(n), not just n (in scenario where observations are independent.

Therefore, for now I have decided to use y_hat for uncertainty evaluation. 

To show how, it would look in real life, here are some examples with real tests.
(picture shows example of [Madrid experiment|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/MP/pages/4518313985/2023-06+Madrid+iOS+multiple+channels+Budget+Increase]).

# Green line shows the evaluation of uncertainty with y_hat
# Green line shows the evaluation of uncertainty with mu (most often less wide than that of y_hat)
# Yellow dots show, where intervals would land if we just sampled from each day’s posterior. (i.e. assuming independence, which we cannot do because MCMC samples can be dependent)
# Blue line shows how wide intervals would be if we just added the intervals of each separate day (first thing that comes to mind often)
BTW - the scenario where green is wider than the red and yellow is somewhere in between is representative for other countries.

!Uncertainty evaluations.png|width=710,height=511!

[^Check Conf intervals - all.zip]


*Step 3: Compare uncertainty and result for Causal Impact vs PyMC.*
We compared 10 tests to check if we have difference in decision making and credible intervals of Causal Impact vs Linear PyMC model.
 
CIs tend to be much lower for Linear PyMC model (often 1.5-2, but sometimes 3 times smaller)
(see *Comparing_CI* tab)

Thank you Tarmo. To avoid an actual hearing/interview could we share of how the data is ingested but slightly less detailed and standardised? My suggestion below: 

Here is some information on how card data is ingested and used in our platform. :

* User adds payment instrument in the application by entering card details into relevant form
* Application posts this data to dedicated service platform - [pci.bolt.eu|http://pci.bolt.eu/] - where
** card details are forwarded to card tokenisation service Processout, we receive token that is stored in our platform and this can be used for card transactions without card details by our payment processing system
** card PAN is masked (some digits replaced with “*” according to requirements of the PCI DSS standard) and sent to the backend database along with token received in previous step
** our databases store *only* masked data along with card expiration date and owners name as entered in the form
* If we want to change anything in the system by exposing full card details anywhere else in the system or where the data itself is processed-stored, will fall automatically under the scope of PCI compliance requirements

We have chosen to minimise the PCI scope and keep in our databases only the data that is absolutely minimal to do business (process payments) and we mask sensitive data in order to be compliant with PCI DSS and GDPR.

Reviewed the agreement and included some substantial changes.

 I believe there is high risk that the online identifiers which the provider may potentially have access to could amount to personal data as they could allow for the identification of an individual. Better safe than sorry.

1] As such, just in case PD is processed, I added C2C basic clauses - considering the identifiers are standard Google Analytics, it should not be particularly high risk, and much easier than making them to sign a DSA from our side.

C2C and not C2P relation - due to the fact that Delve would like to use “aggregated” data for their own purposes - however: 1. We cannot make sure that this data is anonymised - even if so, it could be prone to extraction attacks; 2. just the act of anonymising it in case the standard scope of PD would amount to processing for their purposes, making them a controller; 3. its much easier to agree on a C2C arrangement for them, as our DPA standards are pretty high.

2] Also - removed the requirement to inform the DS and collect consent - it's our own obligation and should have nothing to do with DELVE, if my understanding of the arrangement is correct. So no point in keeping this in the contract.

3] Changed the liability in clause 8 to mutual - they will probably push back, lets see.

I reviewed the 9 Jan version of the agreement (Ancoris’s comments) and need your input on the following commercial points (see below). 

Ancoris has once more declined certain suggestions from our previous round without providing any commentary on the reasons for rejecting the clauses. This practice of outright rejection without explanation is counterproductive and hinders progress in negotiations. 

*Given that numerous outstanding points relate to commercial review* (i.e. not legal review and thus I cannot take decisions on these points and need to seek your input), *it would be greatly appreciated if going forward, you could assess the comments from the other party before forwarding the agreement to me.* This can be conveniently accomplished by thoroughly reviewing all counterparty comments and incorporating your reflections as ‘internal comments’ to the agreement document. This approach would be time-efficient, as it obviates the need for me to independently review and seek your input on the commercial aspects, which are outside of the standard legal review (and thus I cannot take any decisions on these points myself and need to seek your input).

*Outstanding commercial points* that still need to be negotiated with Ancoris are the following:

*1) Ancoris insists on keeping the MSA general and not limited to the reselling of Google Maps services.* I pushed back in my 21 Dec review saying 

“_We are not interested in this agreement being treated as the MSA for various services to be agreed upon in future order forms. This agreement will regulate strictly the reselling of Google Maps services. If the parties are interested in negotiating a new agreement in the future, the new agreement will be negotiated separately from this agreement. Thus, relevant wording is reinstated throughout the agreement.”_ 

Ancoris continues to disagree saying _“We understand your position,_ *_but that is not the way this arrangement works in practice. Ancoris is a reseller, not a direct provider of Google software. We also only operate via an MSA._*_”_ 

To be honest, I don’t understand at all what this statement is supposed to mean? *In my view their arguments are completely unfounded - probably the only reason they are pushing for the MSA is the fact that if we sign a MSA, all future services will fall under the already agreed terms (incl. limitation of liability) - if we agree to the MSA in its current form without limiting it to the services currently ordered, we limit our ability to renegotiate the general terms for future services (incl. limitation of liability).* Please share your views - are we going to order any additional services from them in the future and are you OK with the fact that all these services will be governed by the terms agreed in the current MSA? Perhaps it’s worth revisiting this topic with them and asking them to clarify why they are so difficult.

*2)  Clause 4.2. - Ancoris has refused to inform Bolt of any updates to the service terms* - please let me know whether you are OK with the fact that they have deleted the obligation to inform. Driver/courier is eligible for a cashout and sees the active _Early cashout_ button in their app only if all of the following conditions are met:

* They have completed at least 25 trips/orders during the last 2 months
* Their account is active
* There isn’t any irregular activity detected associated with their account
* They don’t have a transaction in progress
* They are compliant with our [Terms and Conditions|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/]
* They are enrolled in the test (If the feature is not fully rolled out in the market).

Once there is no irregular activity detected by the system, he will be able to see the button again in the app. Please check the [procedure|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/4402393493138], you will find more details there, as there is no need to escalate such cases to the Fraud Team.

Ioana

Hi [~accountid:620363df9493720070b86c71] it is recommended that you consider the following two topics:

*a) do I need to have prior licence from public authority?*

_In the case of publicity in the windows, it would appear that no prior licence would be required as long as the publicity is on Bolt Market. Given that the municipality may have specific requirements, I would recommend that you contact the town council to confirm that in the specific case no licence is needed and whether the publicity complies with the requirements._ _Legal details below._

Law no. 97/88 of 17 August ("Display and inscription of advertising and propaganda messages") stipulates that the display or inscription of advertising messages requires prior authorisation from the competent authorities (usually the town councils), except in the following cases:

* When the advertising is affixed to or inscribed on property that they own or legitimately possess and is *not visible* or audible from the public space;
* When the advertising is affixed to or inscribed on property that they own or legitimately possess and the message publicises *the name or brand of the establishment or respective business or is related to goods or services commercialised in the building in which they are located*, even if they are *visible* or audible from the public space;
* When the advertisement occupies the public space adjacent to the *façade* of the establishment and publicises the name or brand of the establishment or its business or is related to goods or services marketed in the establishment.

Municipalities are responsible for defining the criteria that must be observed when displaying and inscribing advertising messages that are not subject to licensing. In Porto, the criteria are set out in the Regulatory Code of the Municipality of Porto (Annex D2).

*b) do I need to have prior authorization from the landlord?*

It would appear that is not required for publicity in window (inside the store) since we have a lease agreement that specifically indicates we aim to use the propriety for our business purposes. It is settled in the jurisprudence that landlord must collaborate in good faith to allow the comercial use of the property.

HI

This is the result of the dynamic commission, the calculation of monthly commission does this way that  we are taking less commission from the driver because we are subtracting from the total Fee (App orders) - all bonuses/compensations/ride discounts

To calculate ride discounts ( need to export all orders for the same period and calculated the difference between the client payed and the ride price)

This is due to a new invoicing system we gradually started to adopt in mid-2022 called Dynamic Commission. Drivers' or Fleets' bonuses are now aggregated in their commission and the final sum is displayed only as one row: commission row. For example;

Commission: 100€, Bonuses 25€, Booking Fee 15€, Refunds 10€

Driver will only see a single row in their commission invoice in the amount of 50€ (100-25-15-10).

So, technically [actual commission - bounses/compensations - rider discounts - booking fees = commission on the invoice]

the report show the gross commission (the report shows the commission before all these discounts). on the invoice, the amount is all other things deducted from it (since commission netting is active). So actual commission invoice will never match with report.

Basically:

Commission invoice - the final sum of commission that  shows for the monthly period, how much commission we took from the driver in the end (after refunds, some of their bonuses/compensation, and rider discounts have been deducted- so this is Driver’s expenses this done to decrease Driver’s commission in the end.

But report and app expenses, shows gross amount that that driver owes to us before we deduct refunds/bonuses/compensations/ ride discounts. 

More info about dynamic commission [here|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/3663265890].

In some cases we generate the invoices as “hidden” invoices - they do exist in the system with the subtype “statement” and they are hidden (they are not sent to the riders, they cannot be downloaded from the Rider App and they cannot be downloaded from the Admin Panel either).

First case - the “Send invoice info for cash payment method” option is unchecked on the company’s profile. In this case the invoices are hidden for payment methods where the rider pays directly to the driver on the spot after the ride (cash or card terminal). → your case

Second case - the issuer and the recipient are the same. It’s not legal to issue an invoice to oneself so in case the driver's registry code and the rider’s registry code are identical, the invoice will be hidden.

Hi,

This is simply "negative commission" due to rider incentives netting in Georgia(if commission is negative, then we don't have anything to invoice). What that practically means:

Drivers "compensate" riders for their discounts on our behalf -> we deduct this amount from drivers' commission.

This can cause negative commission when rider discounts are more than drivers'/fleets' commission. For this example fleet: their commission was 687.64€, and the discounted 694.3€. So, they end up with -6.56€ as commission and it cannot be invoiced as its negative.

What's Next?

Drivers/Fleets get their commission invoice once their commission amount exceeds the discounted incentives in their balance. This can be next month, or any other time in the future when the above condition is met.

There is also a [document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MWkiuS-48KCuDR2wXqdhKB7FE5wBDcc3LgCc1jLrfxg/edit] where we've tried to simplify how netting works for fleets.

**

{noformat}conversions_query ="""

WITH partner_data AS (
SELECT
driver_id,
partner_id,
first_finished_order AS partner_activation_datetime
FROM ng_public_spark.etl_partner_data
WHERE driver_id IS NOT NULL AND partner_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1,2,3),

lead_data AS (
SELECT
fdrl.created AS lead_created_date,
fdrl.id AS lead_id,
fdrl.driver_id, 
fdrl.is_duplicate AS lead_is_duplicate,
admin_city.name AS city, -- registration city
admin_country.name AS country, -- registration country
max(e2.created) AS step_2_created
FROM
ng_public_spark.fleet_driver_registration_log fdrl
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_driver_registration_event e2 ON e2.driver_registration_log_id=fdrl.id AND e2.step='step_2' AND e2.created >= fdrl.created
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city admin_city ON admin_city.id = fdrl.city_id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_country admin_country ON admin_city.country_code  = admin_country.code
WHERE fdrl.created_date >= date('{}')
GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5,6),


combined AS (
SELECT
lead_data.*,
partner_data.driver_id,
partner_data.partner_id,
partner_data.partner_activation_datetime,
MIN(lead_created_date) OVER (PARTITION BY partner_id) AS earliest_lead_created_date
FROM lead_data
LEFT JOIN partner_data ON partner_data.driver_id = lead_data.driver_id
),


combined_2 AS (
SELECT
combined.*,
date_diff(date(partner_activation_datetime),date(earliest_lead_created_date)) AS lead_to_activation_days
FROM combined)



SELECT
date(lead_created_date) AS date,
combined_2.country,
combined_2.city,
count(DISTINCT lead_id) AS signups,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN step_2_created IS NOT NULL THEN lead_id END) AS step_2,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date AND lead_to_activation_days <= 14 THEN partner_id END) AS activations_14d,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date AND lead_to_activation_days <= 21 THEN partner_id END) AS activations_21d,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date AND lead_to_activation_days <= 30 THEN partner_id END) AS activations_30d,
count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN partner_activation_datetime IS NOT NULL AND lead_created_date = earliest_lead_created_date THEN partner_id END) AS activations
FROM combined_2

Hi [~accountid:5f896ba356eec000768527be] 

Getting back to you regarding Romanian and Kenyan agreements:

* Romania - As a matter of principle, the visa/ residence permit expenses could be included in the repayment agreement under the same legal conditions and limitations detailed previosuly in relation to the relocation expenses. Specifically, the expenses incured by the immigration paperwork and assumed by Bolt could be subject to the repayment mechanism under the reserve that such clause may pose enforcement issues in front of the court in terms of recovering the pro rata amount should the employee leave before the end of the restricted period. As regards implementation, in case the employee is relocated from another jurisdiction and requires immigration formalities as well, the wording for the recovery of the immigration expenses (together with the relocation costs) could be added directly into the relocation agreement, by way of slight wording adjustments) and form a single legal instrument. Alternatively, to the extent Bolt would like to regulate only the reimbursement of immigration formalities costs, the draft relocation agreement could be adapted to reflect such situation.
* Kenya - there is no bar preventing an employer and employee from mutually deciding to prorate the fees for the issuance of a work permit. This arrangement ensures that the employer covers the fee proportionate to the employee's continued employment. This means that if the employee leaves employment before the expiration of the work permit period, they are required to reimburse the company for the unused duration of the permit. The difficulty in implementing this provision for employees already under existing employment agreements lies in the necessity to consult and obtain their agreement for the proposed changes in terms and conditions in accordance with Section 10(5) of the Employment Act, 2007. To achieve this, the modification regarding the prorated work permit fee should be presented in a separate document to the affected employees, and the employees must sign the document to indicate their acceptance of the revised terms and conditions.

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *16/12/2023.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 



As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.



We are sharing a copy of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *account data*



For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at  [https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/en-mt/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|smart-link] , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.



*Your rights* 



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.



Yours sincerely,

Bolt

We can either (1) cooperate and provide the information or (2) refuse to provide it. If we choose option (2), the provision in § 205 applies, i.e. the police needs decision from the prosecution in order for us to be legally obligated to provide the information. However, going with option (2) may potentially end up in a dawn raid from the police.

What you you mean too much, actually drivers discounts and compensations decreased his amount on the invoice



This is the result of the dynamic commission, the calculation of monthly commission does this way that  we are taking less commission from the driver because we are subtracting from the total Fee (App orders) - all bonuses/compensations/ride discounts

To calculate ride discounts ( need to export all orders for the same period and calculated the difference between the client payed and the ride price)

This is due to a new invoicing system we gradually started to adopt in mid-2022 called Dynamic Commission. Drivers' or Fleets' bonuses are now aggregated in their commission and the final sum is displayed only as one row: commission row. For example;

Commission: 100€, Bonuses 25€, Booking Fee 15€, Refunds 10€

Driver will only see a single row in their commission invoice in the amount of 50€ (100-25-15-10).

So, technically [actual commission - bounses/compensations - rider discounts - booking fees = commission on the invoice]

*Does my advice cover both agency and principal model options? (Project Blue Risk)*

From my understanding Bolt is no longer changing the business model to an agency model, therefore this question is not applicable. 

*Does my advice factor in IC and WS classification? (Reclassification Risk)*

Generally, Bolt should avoid offering drivers any incentives that are indicative of integration into Bolt. The reason is, if Bolt provides insurance for drivers this may raise questions about the true working relationship between drivers and Bolt. When a court is assessing the employment status of an individual several factors are considered: 

* Control over Work
* Tools and Equipment
* Training
* Risk of Profit or Loss
* Exclusive Relationship

If Bolt offers an extra layer of insurance protection to drivers then this may fall under the category of Bolt providing the driver with the “Tools and Equipment” to carry out their role. This is because independent contractors typically use their own tools and equipment. By Bolt offering an additional layer of insurance it may be considered that Bolt is providing drivers with tools, equipment, or materials, this may then suggest an employer-employee relationship. The court will look beyond what the actual contract says between Bolt and the Driver and will look holistically at what is happening in reality. 

*Does my advice need to be checked with the PP team (Sefton/Regs Risk)?*

Once I was sure I understand PyMC logic and uncertainty evaluations, I started to launch tests with real data.

*Step 1: Generate fake experiments dates*

Collected a set of random dates and markets to generate fake experiments: [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1AO8oWyyKvrCcg8b9laKuv3XXufWx05a6lYk8EOaXM8o/edit#gid=0|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1AO8oWyyKvrCcg8b9laKuv3XXufWx05a6lYk8EOaXM8o/edit#gid=0|smart-link] 

*Step 2: Running tests with Android = constant*iOS assumption*

Then I started running the tests only with the assumption of Android = constant*iOS. 

Even though I trained the model on different periods, I always had some systematic error in the result resulting in a False Positive. And interestingly, this error was going always in one direction.

See some examples here:

[^28-56_days_experiments_20240114_161055.zip]

I was thinking whether the reason is seasonality or non-linear relations of Android and iOS (like Android = const*(iOS^degree)), but it did not confirm.

However, what I saw when I analyzed the residuals was that the error is often systematically skewed. 

!Screenshot 2024-01-16 at 13.52.18.png|width=561,height=687!

This means that Android and iOS are most probably not related by *Android = constant*iOS*, but are converging or diverging with time (i.e. there’s trend). 

*Step 3: Including trend to the model*

Given Android and iOS are diverging with time, including a trend to the model should be able to solve this.

Indeed, I started running the experiments and found that with trend included to the model, we get different results depending on the trained model. Also, there often is a model that does to generate systematic error (that we would choose as the one to use in our framework).

Additionally we see that once trend is added to the model, there’s no systematic prediction error.

!Lagos - different results with trend.png|width=1728,height=1117!

See some examples here:

[^Examples with trend.zip]



*Step 4: So given trend is root of the problem, what is the best way to choose the model?*

First option I thought about was to continue to find the model which best fits the pre-period. 

However, this approach might have a disadvantage - the thing is that if the trend has been changing for some time already, then you are just *lucky* to have the model with the same trend. I.e. with same success you could have  just fitted the pre-period data.

Other approach could be, on the contrary, trying to catch the period of the latest trend. If you manage to catch this period, it can work as additional proof of the fact that the trend is established and going for some time.



But this can also be achieved in two ways:

# Find the period of the latest trend. Cut two weeks of pre-test. Make sure that there’s no systematic error on pre-test
# Just find the latest trend model and train the model on all of it. With no pre-test. And extrapolate it across the test period.

Both periods take an assumption that the established trend will continue over the test period.

However, the second approach takes pre-test dates to learning, which can help decrease the credible intervals.

Hi all,HMRC has handed in the Application for permission to appeal the FTT decision today, so this saga continues. Bolt does not have an opportunity to reply to the Application, so we will have to wait to see what Judge Sinfield decides.The Tribunal Rules require him to make the decision on it as soon as practicable. Depending on how busy the Judge is, he is likely to release this decision within the next 2 – 4 weeks. Deloitte says that because the decision the Judge issued in December of last year raises new points of law, they believe the Judge will give permission to [appeal.In|http://appeal.In] very broad terms, HMRC has applied for permission on the following grounds:

* Because the Tribunal erred in law by finding Bolt’s supplies fell within TOMS just by being a form of passenger transport.
* That the Tribunal erred in law in considering that Bolt’s supplies fell within TOMS because some trips were made to and from places where Tour Operators generally transport people.
* Because the Tribunal erred in considering that, if a multiplicity of services or features was needed for the supplies to fall within TOMS, Bolt provided these.
* That the Tribunal erred in rejecting HMRC’s contention that the supplies were materially altered or were in house supplies.

We'll deep dive to the Appeal in the coming days and keep you posted if anything material or surprising pops up from it.

Organic Law 6/1985, of the Judiciary, establishes in its articles 17. “1. All public and private persons and entities are obliged to provide, in the manner established by law, the collaboration required by the Judges and Courts in the course of the process and in the execution of the resolution,” in relation to art. 550. “1. In criminal investigation functions, the Judicial Police will act under the direction of the courts and tribunals and the Public Prosecutor's Office. …” and art. 549.1 correspond specifically to the Judicial Police Units, the functions of a) The investigation about the
responsible and circumstances of the criminal acts and arrest of the former, where it is then reported to the judicial and fiscal authority, in accordance with
the provisions of the laws………

Organic Law 2/1986, on Forces and Security, establishes in article 34.2 “In the proceedings or actions carried out, by order and under the
supervision of the competent Criminal Judges, Courts or Prosecutors, the officials who are members of the Judicial Police Corps Units
They will have the status of commissioners of said Judges, Courts and Prosecutors, and may require the necessary assistance from the Authorities and, where appropriate, from the
individuals.”
Royal Decree 769/1987, on the regulation of the Judicial Police, provides in its article 13 that “In the proceedings or actions carried out
by order and under the supervision of the competent Judges, Courts or Prosecutors, the officials who are members of the Organic Units of the Police
Judicial will have the character of commissioners of those and, in this capacity, they may require the necessary assistance from the authorities and, where appropriate, from the
individuals.”

Organic Law 7/2021, of May 26, on the protection of personal data processed for the purposes of prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution
of criminal infractions and the execution of criminal sanctions, establishes in its article 7, the duty of collaboration of public Administrations, as well as
Any natural or legal person will provide the data, reports, background information and supporting documents to the competent authorities that request them, provided that these
are necessary for the specific development of their missions for the prevention, detection and investigation of criminal offenses and for the prevention and protection
facing a real and serious danger to public safety. The request from the competent authority must be concrete and specific and contain the motivation that
prove its relationship with the indicated assumptions.
The interested party will not be informed of the transmission of their data to the competent authorities, nor of having facilitated access to them by said authorities.
authorities in any other way, in order to guarantee the investigative activity.
In accordance with art. 4 of Organic Law 7/2021, the Security Forces and Bodies, among which is the institution of the Civil Guard, such as
State Security Force and Corps, is considered the Competent Authority, for the purposes of the aforementioned Organic Law 7/2021.-
The personal data transferred will be kept by the person responsible for the treatment, only for the time necessary to fulfill the purposes of
prevention, detection and investigation of criminal offenses and for the prevention and protection against a real and serious danger to public safety. or in your
case, they will be diligently incorporated into the report prepared by this Unit, as established by the current Criminal Procedure Law (Art. 282 and
following).-

ALSO, YOU ARE INFORMED that in accordance with art. 58 section j, of Law 7/2021, the refusal to provide the competent authorities with the
information necessary for the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offenses, for the execution of criminal sanctions or for the
protection and prevention against threats against public security in accordance with the provisions of article 7, as well as to inform the interested party when

{color:#4c9aff}+*GENERAL INFORMATION ON CHARITABLE DONATIONS*+{color}

When a company collects charitable donations from consumers, transparency and clarity are essential. 

Key considerations for ensuring clarity in the collection of charitable payments include: 

* *Purpose of the Donation*
* *Use of Funds*
* *Fees and Administrative Costs*
* *Legal Compliance*
* *Receipts and Confirmations*
* *Privacy and Security*

Generally companies are expected to provide clear information about how the funds are collected, how the funds will be used and any fees or administrative costs associated with the donation process. I have reviewed the attached links and reviewed how this would look from the passengers perspective on the app, whilst I appreciate that there is an information button next to the category “The Bike Project” (and I am assuming, correct me if I am wrong that this info button contains all information relating to the charitable donation outlined on this link [here|https://bolt.eu/en-gb/blog/give-the-gift-of-mobility-to-the-bike-project-with-bolt/]) I do not think that from a consumer end that it is clear that a consumer would be charged a 50p donation. For transparency purposes so the user is clear on their choices when selecting the categories on the app, it may be better to have a one liner underneath the category saying something along the lines of for example (not this exact wording) _“select this category if you want to make a 0.50p charitable donation to the Bike Project see here for more information”._ This will ensure that the passenger (the donor) makes an informed decision on whether they want to allocate charitable contributions. 

It is important for companies to be as transparent as possible, this ensures that the company can build trust with their consumers and demonstrate their commitment to ethical and responsible charitable practices. 

h4. {color:#4c9aff}+*Risks for not being transparent to consumers on collection charitable donations*+ {color}

Failure to be transparent when collecting charitable donations can expose companies to various risks, such as: legal, reputational, Loss of Consumer Trust, Decreased Consumer Engagement, Customer Boycotts, Regulatory Scrutiny, Employee Morale and Retention.

Thanks for checking [~accountid:62d01789bd54f8d3ffb6c03d]. That’s correct it’s not sufficient. I believe you (and the court might _understand_) +*but*+ court decisions are +*only*+ based on what can be proved with evidence, some more details for you below.

+*Why are Jose’s claims not evidence?*+ 

For all the court knows he might be claiming more in the email than what they had actually agreed from the start. If we can’t prove what was contracted, it’s almost impossible to win a breach of contract-case in court. It’s word against word. 

In Thomas reply he countered Jose’s claims with the opposite facts, he says they have done everything as agreed / standard practice / instructions from Jose. *I’m not saying Thomas is right. He probably isn’t. We just can’t prove that.*

+*If we don’t have a written agreement, why can’t the court go with the email?*+

Based on only the email, a court couldn’t for sure decide if Jose was (1) mad because he entered into a bad agreement or (2) listing valid contract breaches. |*Data processing question*|*Bolt*|*Partner restaurant*|
|*Who determines the purpose of the processing (i.e., the why)?*|Bolt processes client’s (Bolt Food user) personal data mainly to offer information society service i.e., Bolt Food to the client; and to offer information society service to the partner restaurant. By doing so Bolt has its own purpose for processing personal data. Bolt has determined purpose of processing and qualifies as a controller of personal data.|Partner restaurant processes client’s personal data to enter into and fulfil sales agreement (sale of food/preparation of food). Partner restaurant has its own purpose of processing personal data that is a separate and different purpose compared to Bolt’s data processing purposes. |*Who determines the means of processing (i.e., the how)?*|Bolt offers information society service to both the client and the partner restaurant. By doing so Bolt qualifies as controller of personal data regards to Bolt’s relevant information society service.|Partner restaurant has decided to use certain service provider (i.e., Bolt) in aiding the partner restaurant to connect with its clients. This means that the partner restaurant has made a general decision on how the personal data is being processed. In context with the general situation of the processing the partner restaurant qualifies as the controller of personal data in providing its own service even if they use service provider for aiding their service provision.|
|*CONCLUSION:*|Bolt is data controller when providing its relevant information society service. Bolt does not process data on behalf of partner restaurant.|Partner restaurant is data controller while using Bolt service when offering its own services.
