Hey,

I understand your problem but it would cause unreasonable extra workload and risks. 


I’ll explain my concern.

We use REF-IDs when booking manual journals with EIB templat. On average 17-22K lines of accounting input is booked with source “manual journal” on a monthly basis. We have ca 40 legal entities and I think 100 people in Finance Dept all together (not all work with journals, but I'm guessing half of them for sure). 
    
Sometimes the person who prepares the data is not the same who uploads it; in this case the 2nd person should check the correctness of the file - this would be much more difficult with numerical values. 

We have also built controls into Workday as critical validations - to detect and fix dimension mismatches. Basically one can’t post the journal without fixing logic errors.

Below is one example of EIB we upload to Workday to book journals (these templates are sometimes hundreds of lines long). Let's say there are following errors (highlighted in red) :
1) CC vs BL mismatch - currently it’s easy to see for human eye that CC *CS-Rides* vs BL *Restaurant* is the problem. If it would be *CC001* vs *Restaurant*, we would need to perform extra step to look up the value for CC001. 
2) Customer Type vs CC mismatch → currently quite easy to see that CT *Regular* vs CC *DELIVERY-BUSINESS-OPS* has logic error.  If it would be *CC005* vs CT *Regular*, we would need to perform extra step to look up the value for CC005. 
These are some examples.
 

IPO readiness is the main goal for finance this year (as for many teams I guess). For finance this means decreasing month end closing time significantly (from 6 → 5 → 3 days within next year). And all this while increasing quality 😄 .


So I do understand your problem and it makes sense to me when looking at it from isolated scope. But when looking at the bigger picture, I’d say the additional work and inconvenience this change would cause does not outweigh the benefits.

I understand it’s an inconvenience for people who need to manually update or fix reports when some ID-s change (I personally also struggle with this). But on the others we have about 40 active legal entities, let say 50 people in finance and 20K lines we need to book with manual journals on a regular monthly basis - this would be much bigger inconvenience.

Hey [~accountid:625c10eb9506d6006fd7cf91], please prepare the data for this request and share it with us before it is sent out. Thank you.

+*REVIEW OF PROJECT KODAK*+ 

# {color:#ff991f}*CCTV PARTNERSHIP* {color}

Bolt will be acting as an introducer, introducing the driver to the partner (who offers the CCTV). Bolt will be promoting this benefit to the drivers. 

Intention is for there to be an agreement between Bolt and the Partner, then the Partner will have a separate agreement in place with the Driver. - do you have any draft versions of what the agreement between the partner and Bolt will look like? Will Bolt have sight of the agreement between the partner and the driver, whilst Bolt is not a party to this agreement, it may be helpful to have sight of how this may look. 

You mention that the partner will be providing Bolt with the details on how many vehicles have had CCTV installed and uninstalled. I am assuming that the driver must be providing consent for this information to be shared. 

The privacy team would need to conduct a review on this project and provide comments on the data sharing aspects and if there are any red flags in regards to this. 

+*WHAT HAPPENS IF A SAFETY INCIDENT OCCURS*+ 

You mention that drivers (who will be the data processors) will have the option to provide Bolt with the footage but will not be required to do so. If the driver does not consent the incident will be investigated in the usual way. 

+*WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS TO THE PARTNER COMPANY*+

The partner will  benefit from being alerted if there is an incident having a chance to make offers to the driver on how to manage it. The partner will try to promote other strands of their business to the driver for example: representing the driver for the accident on a “no win no fee basis”, putting the driver in contact with courtesy car companies etc. 

How much does it cost for a driver to get this CCTV installed? 

+*WHAT IS THE INCENTIVE FOR THE DRIVER*+ 

For the driver the incentive is that having CCTV installed in their vehicle can act as a deterrent for any incidents to occur on the journey. It will also help the driver mitigate against any claims made by a passenger. In addition, insurance companies may offer cheaper insurance to drivers on the basis that they have CCTV installed in their vehicle. 

+*DOES THIS HAVE AN EFFECT ON BOTH THE AGENCY AND PRINCIPLE MODEL*+ 

From my understanding Bolt is no longer changing the business model to an agency model, therefore this question is not applicable. 

+*REVIEW OF EXTERNAL ADVICE BOLT HAS RECEIVED TO DATE REGARDING RECLASSIFICATION*+ 

Bolt is advised by Lewis Silkin to avoid any features which would indicate that the driver is integrated into Bolt. See snapshot of advice below: 

h4. “Lewis Silkin advice note - July 2022

(iii) Avoid other features that are indicative of integration: for example, you have referred to access to leased and/or branded vehicles and insurance perks via a funding allowance as a benefit of worker status, but this does not mean you need to compel drivers to use a particular vehicle while working for Bolt, or to take up your insurance offering rather than spending the money elsewhere, and you could make this clear”. 

+*WHAT HAPPENS IF THE DRIVER LEAVES BOLT?*+ 

If the driver stops working for Bolt how will this work? Do the drivers have to have the CCTV uninstalled by the partner or does the driver get to carry on using the CCTV equipment? I raise this question as it is the driver who will be bearing the cost of installing the CCTV. 

+*ARE THERE ANY RECLASSIFICATION RISKS*+ 

In the Uber case, it was determined that drivers should be classified as workers due to various factors, one of which was the significant control exerted by Uber. This control was examined through five key dimensions:

* Financial control
* Contractual control
* Acceptance of riders control
* Scope of services control
* Information control

Drivers are given a choice on whether or not they want to contact the partner provider and install the CCTV in their vehicles as opposed to the drivers being forced to have this in their vehicle. Given that Bolt is not imposing this as a requirement for drivers to use the Bolt platform, there are no major red flags here as there is no ‘contractual control’ being exerted onto the driver.  Bolt is acting as an introducer only (promoting the partner to the driver)*.* 

I would need to review the agreement between Bolt and the CCTV Partner to provide a more deeper analysis. 

Whilst Bolt is not a party to the contract between the driver and the Partner CCTV company, how will it work in terms of the CCTV Partner company providing you statistics on how many drivers have had this installed/uninstalled? I am assuming there will be a clause in the agreement between the driver and the Partner whereby the driver is giving consent for the Partner to share their data with Bolt. 

+*TERMS AND CONDITIONS*+ 

If Project Kodak is given the green light and goes ahead there would need to be a provision where the passengers are consenting to the CCTV, it may be that a provision in the T&Cs needs to be added whereby if the passenger is taking a trip with Bolt they are providing consent to the CCTV, however this needs to be looked into further by the privacy team and how this could be achieved (and if there are any issues from a privacy perspective). 

+*PUBLIC POLICY TEAM*+ 

Has the PP team given sign off on this project?

{color:#36b37e}*2. CCTV SUBSIDY* {color}

Purpose: is to improved safety for both driver and passenger

I have two concerns with this initiative: 

# Bolt subsidising the cost of the CCTV (the installation as well as paying the monthly fee); and 
# This will only be offered to qualified drivers

+*Concern 1*+ 

Generally, Bolt should avoid offering drivers any incentives (subsidising CCTV payments for drivers) that are indicative of integration into Bolt. The reason is, if Bolt provides subsidised payments for drivers this may raise questions about the true working relationship between drivers and Bolt. Independent contractors should maintain autonomy and control over their work, by Bolt paying for drivers CCTV it may be seen as Bolt providing the driver with the resources to work which may create a perception that the contractor is more like an employee, potentially jeopardising the contractor's status as an independent worker. In addition, Subsidising payments for drivers may create an expectation that Bolt is providing additional benefits (which is traditionally associated with employees) such as health, again blurring the lines between independent contractor and employee relationships.

+*Concern 2*+ 

[Option A] Selected drivers are enrolled in a campaign which will be visible in their app

[Option B] Alternatively, selected drivers are simply contacted by email and/or in-app message with the details of the offer

You mention that only qualified drivers will be eligible for either option A or option B. Bolt selects drivers who are eligible for the campaign, targeting existing *_top drivers_*. Top drivers will be identified based on:

* Number of finished orders within the past 3 months - this will ensure that Bolt's take from these drivers’ activity is already higher than the price for the cameras.
* Activity score (i.e. acceptance X completion rate: calculated based on the last 80 orders that a driver receives within their selected radius. The activity score increases when the driver accepts and completes a trip and decreases when orders are rejected, cancelled, or not responded to).
* Metrics will be city specific (a top driver in London for example would not be considered as a top driver in Birmingham) and monitored monthly.
* Quarterly review will be done to assess the requirements to make sure they are still relevant on a city by city basis.

* The offer will be limited to drivers who are also the vehicle owners (i.e. not renting the vehicle from a rental company / fleet).

By Bolt only allowing top drivers to be included in the campaign as opposed to this being offered to all drivers, this may be construed as Bolt excluding drivers who do not fall within the ‘top drivers’ category. Essentially, if a driver does not complete X amount of trips or maintain an acceptable activity score then the driver would not be considered to meet the threshold of ‘top driver’. This could slip into the realms of contractual control and acceptance of riders control blurring the lines between independent contractor and employee relationships.

Hey [~accountid:5acb1f48d8b95a2b34f150a8] [~accountid:5b7bea6c358c9f2a008eab3e] 

I have now had a look into the Project Kodak overview. I will provide my breakdown of each strand in two comments on this ticket. 

+*REVIEW*+

{color:#4c9aff}First strand - CCTV Partnership{color} 

+*Questions to*+ [~accountid:5acb1f48d8b95a2b34f150a8] / [~accountid:5b7bea6c358c9f2a008eab3e] 

*What happens if a Driver stops working for Bolt?*

If the driver stops working for Bolt how will this work? Do the drivers have to have the CCTV uninstalled by the partner or does the driver get to carry on using the CCTV equipment? I raise this question as it is the driver who will be bearing the cost of installing the CCTV. 

*Privacy review*

There are a few red flags here which would need to be looked into further by the privacy team, in terms of how data will be shared (for example, the partner company providing Bolt data on drivers who have had this installed, the drivers having the CCTV footage etc.) In addition, how Bolt would obtain valid consent from passengers for drivers to record them during the trip, and how consent is provided by passengers (who may not have their own Bolt account). If a Subject Access Request is raised by a   passenger to obtain the footage (following an incident), whilst I appreciate that the driver is the data controller, I envision that these requests would come directly to Bolt. These matters need to be analysed by the privacy team. Cc. [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] 

*Reclassification risks*

In the Uber case, it was determined that drivers should be classified as workers due to various factors, one of which was the significant control exerted by Uber. This control was examined through five key dimensions:

* Financial control
* Contractual control
* Acceptance of riders control
* Scope of services control
* Information control

Drivers are given a choice on whether or not they want to contact the partner provider and install the CCTV in their vehicles as opposed to the drivers being forced to have this in their vehicle. Given that Bolt is not imposing this as a requirement for drivers to use the Bolt platform, there are no major red flags here as there is no ‘contractual control’ being exerted onto the driver.  Bolt is acting as an introducer only (promoting the partner to the driver)*.* 

*Agreement between Bolt and Partner provider*

I would need to review the agreement between Bolt and the CCTV Partner to provide a more deeper analysis. 

Whilst Bolt is not a party to the contract between the driver and the Partner CCTV company, how will it work in terms of the CCTV Partner company providing you statistics on how many drivers have had this installed/uninstalled? I am assuming there will be a clause in the agreement between the driver and the Partner whereby the driver is giving consent for the Partner to share their data with Bolt (to be reviewed by privacy team). 

*Public policy team* 

Has the public policy team giving the green light on this?

{color:#6554c0}Second strand: CCTV subsidy{color}

I have two concerns with this initiative: 

# Bolt subsidising the cost of the CCTV (the installation as well as paying the monthly fee); and 
# This will only be offered to qualified drivers

+*Concern 1*+ 

Generally, Bolt should avoid offering drivers any incentives (subsidising CCTV payments for drivers) that are indicative of integration into Bolt. The reason is, if Bolt provides subsidised payments for drivers this may raise questions about the true working relationship between drivers and Bolt. Independent contractors should maintain autonomy and control over their work, by Bolt paying for drivers CCTV it may be seen as Bolt providing the driver with the resources to work which may create a perception that the contractor is more like an employee, potentially jeopardising the contractor's status as an independent worker. In addition, Subsidising payments for drivers may create an expectation that Bolt is providing additional benefits (which is traditionally associated with employees), again blurring the lines between independent contractor and employee relationships.

+*Concern 2*+ 

*_[Option A] Selected drivers are enrolled in a campaign which will be visible in their app_*

*_[Option B] Alternatively, selected drivers are simply contacted by email and/or in-app message with the details of the offer_*

You mentioned in the overview that only qualified drivers will be eligible for either option A or option B. Bolt selects drivers who are eligible for the campaign, targeting existing *_top drivers_*. Top drivers will be identified based on:

* “Number of finished orders within the past 3 months - this will ensure that Bolt's take from these drivers’ activity is already higher than the price for the cameras.
* Activity score (i.e. acceptance X completion rate: calculated based on the last 80 orders that a driver receives within their selected radius. The activity score increases when the driver accepts and completes a trip and decreases when orders are rejected, cancelled, or not responded to).
* Metrics will be city specific (a top driver in London for example would not be considered as a top driver in Birmingham) and monitored monthly.
* Quarterly review will be done to assess the requirements to make sure they are still relevant on a city by city basis.
* The offer will be limited to drivers who are also the vehicle owners (i.e. not renting the vehicle from a rental company / fleet).”

By Bolt only allowing top drivers to be included in the campaign as opposed to this being offered to all drivers, this may be construed as Bolt excluding drivers who do not fall within the ‘top drivers’ category. Essentially, if a driver does not complete X amount of trips or maintain an acceptable activity score then the driver would not be considered to meet the threshold of ‘top driver’. This could slip into the realms of contractual control and acceptance of rides control, and this is because drivers who do not compete on the same level as ‘top drivers’ would not be considered for the campaign. This could blur the lines between independent contractor and employee relationships. 

*Public policy team*

Has the public policy team giving the green light on this?

*Privacy team* 

For the same reasons mentioned below the Privacy team would need to conduct a review on this. 

Happy to discuss further on a call or on slack if needed.

Additionally, 

* The Tool Reference number will be used as the Client reference # on the Insurance Portal.  

* Automatic Notifications will be sent proactively to the Claimant directly via email from the insurer.  
* We also discussed access controls on their portal for our visibility, they will be getting back to us on some discussed points ( see doc).

Hi Epp,

We revert to you on this topic following our conversation with you and Ilya on Wednesday. Please accept our apologies as we did not manage to get this out as early as we had hoped.

Below we have added *in blue* to the advice previously sent based on your explanations during the call. In short:

·     What you envisage doing can be broken down as follows: *(A) you would be comparing data from Google APIs against data observed on your platform, internally, to allow for determination of a multiplier (e.g., x2) to bridge gaps between data from Google APIs and data observed on Bolt’s platform and (B) ultimately leverage this system to correct/elaborate your Geo Service/ETA map data*. 

·     Our advice had set out the analysis of these two items in light of the applicable Google terms and conditions. We believe *the additional information you provided complements rather than changes the analysis*.

·     On this basis, *we come to the conclusion that our advice stands: with regard to item (A) the short answer to the question of whether the terms prohibit this, is NO, and with regard to item (B) the short answer to the question of whether the terms prohibit this, is YES*.

·     However, you may wish to take a risk-based approach in respect of item (B). With this in mind, *a set of safeguards could be put in place by Bolt in order to mitigate risks*.

We are sending this only to you for now as a preview so that you could confirm when we can send it on to Ilya.

 

Happy to discuss.

 

Thank you,

 

ES team

 

---------------

 

        I.       +Introduction+

 

Bolt uses Google Maps APIs for routing drivers: output data of Google Maps APIs such as travel time and route distance information are used for dispatch decisions and displayed to drivers *(although not directly, the underlying data is never disclosed)*. However, this output data does not take into account Bolt’s business specifics (e.g., drivers’ behaviour, city layout features like taxi lanes, etc.) and thus there may be gaps between travel time and route distance information produced by Google and the actual travel time and route distance observed on Bolt’s platform. To measure this and ultimately improve its *Geo Service/ETA* map data accuracy, Bolt envisages using the output data of Google APIs in its internal machine learning model: *in other words, what Bolt envisages doing is taking the ‘**_results_**’ of Google APIs (e.g., estimated time to travel from A to B) to build a ‘**_model_**’ that ‘**_corrects_**’ the data based on Bolt’s business specifics. In order to avoid any ambiguity, it is worthwhile noting that:*

 

·     *the terms ‘**_results_**’ of Google APIs and ‘output data’ of Google Maps APIs can be used interchangeably to identify the data provided by Google through its APIs. More importantly,* +*under the applicable terms and conditions, these ‘*++*_results_*++*’/’output data’ fall under the scope of ‘Google Maps Content’ which means any content provided through the services (whether created by Google or its third-party licensors), including map and terrain data, imagery, traffic data, and places data (including business listings). Such Google Maps content is subject to the restrictive terms of use we outlined below (for example, customers are prohibited from creating content based on Google Maps content or using Google Maps services or Google Maps content to create features similar to those of Google Maps)*+*.*

 

·     *the ‘**_model_**’ would be a system developed internally by Bolt to compare output data of Google APIs against data observed on Bolt’s platform, internally. The system would allow for determination of a multiplier (e.g., x2) to bridge gaps between output data of Google APIs and data observed on Bolt’s platform.*

 

·     *the act of ‘**_correcting_**’ the data would essentially be using this system to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data.*

 

*In practice, what Bolt envisages doing can be broken down as follows:*

 

(i)          *you would be comparing data from Google APIs against data observed on your platform, internally, to* *allow for determination of a multiplier (e.g., x2) to bridge gaps between output data of Google APIs and data observed on Bolt’s platform*: feed Google content into its internal machine learning model for internal benchmarking purposes; *(“*+*Item (A)*+*”)* and

 

(ii)         *ultimately leverage this system to correct/elaborate your Geo Service/ETA map data* *(“Item (B)”)*.

 

Bolt would like to know whether such practices are in line with the applicable terms and conditions (the “+Google Maps Terms and Conditions+”).

 

We have reviewed the Google Maps Terms and Conditions and have set out below a summary of the key findings of our analysis. Please note that multiple sets of terms form the Google Maps Terms and Conditions including the following which contain relevant clauses that we discuss below: Google Maps Platform Terms of Service, Maps Service Specific Terms and Google Maps/Google Earth Additional Terms of Service. Other set of terms apply (e.g., Google Maps Platform Acceptable Use Policy, Legal Notices for Google Maps/Google Earth and Google Maps/Google Earth APIs), however, we have not identified in these additional clauses directly relevant to the analysis at hand.

 

       II.       +*Item (A):*+ +Use of Google content for internal benchmarking purposes+

 

Google Maps Terms and Conditions do not contain any restriction about internal benchmarking. They only require Google Maps customers to not publicly disclose the result of any comparative testing, benchmarking or evaluation of a Google Maps Service, unless the disclosure includes all information necessary for Google or a third party to replicate the test _(clause 3.2.4 ‘Benchmarking’ of Google Maps Platform Terms of Service)_.

 

*Bolt can therefore, without breaching Google Maps Terms and Conditions or Google’s IP rights, conduct internal comparative tests between its internal services and Google Maps services*.

 

     III.       +*Item (B):*+ +(Re)Use of Google content to enrich its internal map data+ +*functionalities (use Google Maps to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data)*+

 

Google Maps Terms and Conditions explicitly prohibit customers from:

 

(i)          creating content based on Google Maps content _(clause 3.2.3 (c) ‘No Creating Content from Google Maps Content’ of Google Maps Platform Terms of Service)_;

 

(ii)         using Google Maps services or Google Maps content to create features similar to those of Google Maps _(clause 3.2.3 (d) ‘No Re-Creating Google Products or Features’ of Google Maps Platform Terms of Service)_;

 

(iii)        using Google Maps services (including Google Maps APIs or content) “with or near a non-Google Map” _(clause 3.2.3 (e) ‘No Use With Non-Google Maps’ of Google Maps Platform Terms of Service )_; or

 

(iv)        using Google Maps/Google Earth to create or augment any other mapping-related dataset (including a mapping or navigation dataset, business listings database, mailing list, or telemarketing list) for use in a service that is a substitute for, or a substantially similar service to, Google Maps/Google Earth _(clause 2 (d) ‘Prohibited Conduct’ of Google Maps/Google Earth Additional Terms of Service)_.

 

*These restrictions apply both to use of the Google services and use of Google content which (as observed above) covers any content provided through the services and thus includes any output data. On this basis, Bolt’s envisaged practice to (re)use/leverage Google content* *to enrich its internal map data functionalities (use Google Maps to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data)* *appears clearly and unambiguously in conflict with the above restrictions. Bolt should take great caution in respect of such practice as it would entail legal risks and may lead to significant financial implications for Bolt (as explained in more details in section ‘Main risks’ below).*

 

Please note that, with regard to restriction (ii) above (using Google Maps services or Google Maps content to create features similar to those of Google Maps), the terms clarify: “Customer will not use the Services to create a product or service with features that are substantially similar to or that re-create the features of another Google product or service. *Customer’s product or service must contain substantial, independent value and features beyond the Google products or services*.” This wording could be considered as an exception (“provided that”-type provision thereby allowing use of Google Maps services or Google Maps content to create features similar to those of Google Maps). However, erring on the side of caution, we would advise against taking a ‘liberal’ view of this wording and to assess how this may be interpreted in accordance with the governing law (California law) we would have to defer to US counsel.

 

We further note that pursuant to Maps Service Specific Terms (specific terms that apply to APIs such as Directions, Geocoding, Places and Roads APIs), customers can use content from the Directions, Geocoding, Places or Roads APIs without a corresponding Google Map, i.e., without any map. However, we understand that this would not be the case for Bolt in practice as the Google Maps APIs output would be displayed either: (i) on a Google map, or (ii) on its internal map (not without any map)*(although not directly, the underlying data is never disclosed)*. *We further understand that Google Maps APIs output would necessarily continue to be used by Bolt once the project is implemented, even after Bolt has built the envisaged system to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data, as Bolt needs Google Maps APIs output data for routing drivers.*

 

In any case, where internal database creation efforts can be conducted in compliance with Google Maps Terms and Conditions, it is recommended that Bolt carefully documents the process it uses in order to be able to demonstrate this to Google and/or any auditors.

 

    IV.       +Main risks+

 

If Bolt allows *Item B (the (re)use/leverage of Google Maps to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data)*, and Google was to realise this, Google could then try to claim that Bolt has breached the Google Maps Terms and Conditions and/or their IP rights, or that it shall have IP rights on Bolt’s data.

 

·     *Breach of Google Maps Terms and Conditions*: As set out above, the Google Maps Terms and Conditions restrict customers from using Google services without complying with restrictions. Google could, should they realise it, claim that Bolt has breached the Google Maps Terms and Conditions.

 

·     *IP rights could be revendicated by Google*: The Google Maps Terms and Conditions provide that Google owns all IP rights in the Google Maps services and content (clause 6.1 ‘Intellectual Property Rights’ of Google Maps Platform Terms of Service). Google could, should they realise it, claim that Bolt has infringed its IP rights by using proprietary content without complying with licensing terms and/or revendicate IP rights on Bolt’s *Geo Service/ETA* map data.

 

The risk that Google would be able to realise that Bolt’s *Geo Service/ETA* map data may have been elaborated/verified using Google Maps would seem quite low as it would most likely not be discernible by looking at Bolt’s app. *Indeed, there would be no display/disclosure of the system used to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data or any underlying data (including output data of Google Maps APIs which is never disclosed). For this reason, it would most likely be very difficult to identify and reverse engineer.* However, in the event of an audit (a right of audit is granted to Google in the Google Maps Terms and Conditions), Google may request that Bolt submits internal documentation which may indicate that the data comes from/has been verified using Google Maps. Further, in case Google identifies any non-compliance with the restrictions applicable to the Google Maps services, it could, as per the applicable Terms and Conditions, take the following measures against Bolt:

 

·     suspend access to or use of the Google Maps services (including Google Maps APIs and content);

 

·     decide to terminate the license agreement (i.e. permanently remove access to the Google Maps services), after having provided a prior written notice to Bolt and if Bolt fails to correct the breach identified in this notice within 30 days; and/or

 

·     request damages of up to the amount of fees paid by Bolt to Google during the 12 months preceding the event that Google identifies as a breach of Google Maps Terms and Conditions (for reference, the amount paid to Google in 2020 was 3.2 million euros).

 

Please also note that, should Google request an indemnification from Bolt and should the parties fail to find an amicable solution, any dispute would have to be brought, as per Google Maps Terms and Conditions, before the courts of the Santa Clara Country, California, United States. Litigation in the United States generally involves the disclosure of large quantities of information by both parties (during the pre-trial “discovery” phase), and is known to be very expensive.

 

      V.       +*Risk mitigation*+

 

*Bolt may wish to take a risk-based approach in respect of Item (B). As observed above, the risk that Google could identify this by just looking at Bolt’s apps seems to be quite low. With this in mind, Bolt could consider adopting the following set of safeguards to mitigate the risks:*

 

# 

*Ensure output data of Google Maps APIs is kept for no longer than needed to build the envisaged system and permanently erased after.*

 

2.

*To the extent it is technically feasible and compatible with Bolt’s needs, ensure data corrected/elaborated through the system is segregated from output data of Google Maps APIs.*

 

3.

*Never disclose or display in any way whatsoever the system used to correct/elaborate Bolt’s Geo Service/ETA map data or any underlying data.*

 

4.

*Strictly limit knowledge of/access to the system on a need-to-know basis.*

 

5.

*Avoid relying upon an external supplier for any part of the project. Where an external supplier is relied on by Bolt, strong NDA(s) with penalties in the event of a breach by the supplier should be executed between the parties.*

 

6.

*Carefully document Geo Service/ETA map data creation efforts conducted independently and processes used in this respect in order to be able to demonstrate this to Google and/or any auditors.*

script:

{noformat}--- input --
SELECT driver_first_name
	,driver_last_name
	,driver_id
	,taxi_reg_number
	,company_name
	,comapany_reg_code
	,company_email
	,driver_phone
	,driver_email
	,city
	,sum(cash_sum) AS cash_sum
	,sum(in_app_sum) AS in_app_sum
	,sum(ride_price) AS ride_price
	,sum(price) as price
	,sum(distance) / 1000 AS total_distance_1
FROM (
	SELECT otd.first_name AS driver_first_name
		,otd.last_name AS driver_last_name
		,ot.driver_id AS driver_id
		,fc.car_transport_licence_number AS taxi_reg_number
		,fco.company_name AS company_name
		,fco.reg_code AS comapany_reg_code
		,fco.email AS company_email
		,fdjdr.phone AS driver_phone
		,fdjdr.email AS driver_email
		,ot.ride_price AS ride_price
		,ot.price  as price
		,CASE 
			WHEN o.payment_method_type <> 'default'
				THEN ot.ride_price 
			ELSE 0
			END AS in_app_sum
		,CASE 
			WHEN o.payment_method_type = 'default'
				THEN ot.ride_price 
			ELSE 0
			END AS cash_sum
		,city.name AS city
		,ot.distance as distance
	FROM PUBLIC.company_order o
	left join PUBLIC.company_order_try AS ot on ot.order_id =o.id and ot.city_id =o.city_id 
	LEFT JOIN PUBLIC.company_order_try_driver AS otd ON (ot.city_id = otd.city_id AND ot.id = otd.order_try_id)
	LEFT JOIN fleet_car AS fc ON (fc.id = ot.driver_car_id)
	LEFT JOIN fleet_company AS fco ON (fco.id = ot.driver_company_id)
	LEFT JOIN fleet_driver_join_driver_root fdjdr ON (fdjdr.id = ot.driver_id)
	LEFT JOIN admin_system_city city ON ot.city_id = city.id
	WHERE city.country_code = 'no'
		AND convert_timezone(timezone, ot.created) >= '2022-01-01'
		AND convert_timezone(timezone, ot.created) < '2023-01-01'
		AND ot.STATE in ('finished','client_cancelled')
		--AND fco.company_name = 'Arrangement Oslo AS'
		--and otd.last_name='Daiob'
		and 
		and ot.retry_to_try is null
	)
GROUP BY 1

Hey [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3] ,



Thanks for reviewing the document and for providing us with a detailed breakdown of the two initiatives. To answer your questions:

{color:#4c9aff}First strand - CCTV Partnership{color}


*What happens if a Driver stops working for Bolt?*

Drivers will pay an upfront fee for the camera (£69) after which they will own the device. Within the agreement between the driver and the Partner, there will be a minimum commitment period (6 months) during which the driver also needs to pay the weekly fee to the partner (£3.49). After the commitment period has passed, the driver has the option to either continue with the weekly payments or cancel at any time - in which case they will still keep the camera. The weekly fee collected by the partner is more of a service fee (for the processing and storage of data, driver support, etc.) rather than for the device itself. 

*Privacy review*

I will get in touch with the Privacy team and have all the aspects you raised thoroughly reviewed. 

On the topic of the passenger's consent - as Bolt will be promoting the partnership but not technically running it/providing the cameras, how would this differ from situations where drivers have installed a CCTV in their vehicle (either from their initiative or as part of Uber’s scheme for example)? Also, Bolt will not have any access to the footage. 

*Agreement between Bolt and Partner provider*

This is currently TBC but I will make sure to circle back to you when a contract is drafted. 

As for the contract between the driver and the Partner and the consent to share the data with Bolt - what you described is our assumption as well. Even though Bolt is not a party to that contract, I would like us to have a sight of it before the offer goes live - so unless you foresee any issues with that, I will probably circle back to you with that as well. 

*Public policy team*

Yes, we are working closely with [~accountid:712020:7da8a66c-8a7e-4912-b329-35d94607bdc3] from the public policy team and keep her updated on both initiatives.



{color:#6554c0}Second strand: CCTV subsidy{color}

I’m not sure if that changes anything, but to clarify: the idea of the subsidy is to pay for the device upfront and in full. Drivers would then go to the selected supplier to get the device installed and would simply pick it up for free - and the supplier would invoice Bolt instead. There would be no monthly payments (as no service or processing of the data will be provided by Bolt - these arrangements would sit with the driver). 

I understand the concern with the selective approach to drivers. Unfortunately, we don’t foresee being able to offer CCTV subsidy to all drivers, mainly due to associated costs and a low ROI.

With the above in mind, how likely do you think it is that we will be able to run the CCTV subsidy? I understand your concerns but I’m also trying to understand the severity of these concerns - where does it sit on a scale between a risk that we can take and a risk that we would *definitely* not take as a business? 

We would aim to launch the subsidy around Q3 this year so there is still enough time to discuss potential modifications that would mitigate the risks. The priority for now is the CCTV partnership which we’d like to launch in March.

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

*Your rights*

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

Yours sincerely,

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *13/12/2023.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.



We are sharing a copy of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.



Yours sincerely,

Bolt
